result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.boundary_expansion()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the boundary (vertex) expansion of a set of nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L41822-L41864){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.boundary_expansion(S) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Boundary expansion](/assets/graphs/boundary-expansion.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same graph and set S. Only neighbors outside S count: D and E, in accent, each touch the triangle. Two outside neighbors over three members gives boundary expansion 2 / 3 = 0.667." width="100%"} The number of nodes *outside* the set that are adjacent to it (its node boundary, see `node_boundary()`) divided by the size of the set. This is the vertex expansion of expander-graph theory: in a good expander, every small set has many outside neighbors, so information spreads quickly and no small group can be isolated by removing few nodes. On a directed graph, neighbors are nodes the set points to. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [S]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The nodes, as integer IDs or string labels. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The boundary expansion. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `S=` is empty or a node does not exist. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The hub of a star reaches every leaf, so its boundary is as large as the graph allows: ::: {#61746d5d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec star = ec.Graph().add_star_graph(5) star.boundary_expansion([1]), star.boundary_expansion([2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (4.0, 1.0) ``` ::: :::
